claims.claim: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, tested in deep sleep, the standard high-pitched (3100 Hz) smoke alarm at 75 dBA woke 56%, while a lower-pitched 520 Hz square-wave signal at the same level woke 92%.
claims.supporting_passage: Three auditory signals, a bed shaker, a pillow shaker, and strobe lights were presented to 38 adults (aged 18 to 80 yr) with mild to moderately severe hearing loss of 25 to 70 dB (in both ears), during slow-wave sleep (deep sleep). ... The third auditory signal was the current 3100-Hz smoke alarm. All auditory signals were tested below, at, and above the decibel level prescribed by the applicable standard for bedrooms (75 dBA). ... The most effective signal was a 520-Hz square wave auditory signal, waking 92% at 75 dBA, compared with 56% waking to the 75 dBA high-pitched alarm.
claims.pico_timeframe: 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with hearing loss 25 to 70 dB / 520 Hz square wave, bed and pillow shakers, strobe / standard 3100 Hz alarm / woken (EEG) during slow-wave sleep / laboratory nights (number not given in abstract)
claims.safe_wording: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, a standard high-pitched smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 of them from deep sleep. A lower-pitched alarm sound at the same loudness woke about 92 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Say who was studied: adults of all ages (18 to 80), not only older people; laboratory, deep sleep only; small sample. The abstract does not state whether hearing aids were worn; frame the post conditionally ('if you take your hearing aids out at night') rather than claiming participants had removed them. Do not tell readers to buy a 520 Hz alarm: UK availability was not checked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting study found. The authors' conclusion that low-frequency signals work better in several other groups (including older adults) refers to their other work, which was not opened here.

numbers.meaning: participants, aged 18 to 80, hearing loss 25 to 70 dB in both ears
proportion woken by the standard 3100 Hz alarm at 75 dBA, deep sleep
proportion woken by the 520 Hz square-wave signal at 75 dBA, deep sleep
loudness set by the applicable bedroom standard

claims.claim: In the same study, bed and pillow shakers woke 80 to 84% at the intensity as purchased, while strobe lights woke only 27% even at an intensity above the US standard.
claims.supporting_passage: In the case of bed and pillow shakers intensities below, at, and above the level as purchased were tested. For strobe lights three levels were used, all of which were above the applicable standard. ... Bed and pillow shakers awoke 80 to 84% at the intensity level as purchased. The strobe lights awoke only 27% at an intensity above the US standard. ... Strobe lights, even at high intensities, are ineffective in reliably waking people with mild to moderate hearing loss.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-13-a
claims.safe_wording: A vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress woke about 80 to 84 in 100 of the same people. A flashing strobe light woke about 27 in 100, even when brighter than the US standard.
claims.qualifications: Same population and laboratory caveats as C11-13-a. The shakers were tested 'as purchased', so they were commercial products at the time (2009). Use this to say: if you are offered an alarm kit for hearing loss, check it includes a vibrating pad and not only a flashing light.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: proportion woken by bed or pillow shakers at the intensity as purchased
proportion woken by strobe lights at an intensity above the US standard

claims.claim: UK fire and rescue services offer free home fire safety visits (England: all services offer them).
claims.supporting_passage: James and Clark 2025: "All English fire services offer 'Home Fire Safety Visits', designed to help those vulnerable to fire identify and reduce risk at home however, only four specify that people living with dementia are eligible." Hampton 2025: "The UK Fire and Rescue Service (FRS) routinely deliver Home Fire Safety Visits (HFSVs) in people's homes. HFSVs offer support with fire safety and a range of health-related issues." Cockayne 2025: "Fire and rescue services in England routinely carry out Home Fire Safety Visits which aim to reduce risk of fire, support independent living and improve quality of life."
claims.pico_timeframe: English fire and rescue service websites (James and Clark); UK service staff (Hampton); England (Cockayne); 2024 to 2025
claims.safe_wording: Fire and rescue services in the UK carry out home fire safety visits; in England every service offers them. You can ask for one and say that you are hard of hearing.

claims.claim: The 2025 AASM guideline says all patients with clinically significant restless legs should have iron studies (ferritin and transferrin saturation), and that iron should be given if ferritin is 75 ng/mL or less or transferrin saturation is below 20% (and only intravenously if ferritin is 75 to 100 ng/mL); these thresholds are consensus that has not been empirically tested.
claims.supporting_passage: "In all patients with clinically significant RLS, clinicians should regularly test serum iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation (calculated from iron and total iron binding capacity). Testing should ideally be administered in the morning avoiding all iron-containing supplements and foods at least 24 hours prior to blood draw. ... Consensus guidelines, which have not been empirically tested, suggest that supplementation of iron in adults with RLS should be instituted with oral or IV iron if serum ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%, and only with IV iron if serum ferritin is between 75 and 100 ng/mL. ... These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population."
claims.location: Abstract, Good Practice Statement 1 (also page 140 of PDF)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with clinically significant restless legs syndrome; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: A 2025 US sleep medicine guideline (AASM) advises checking ferritin and transferrin saturation in everyone with troublesome restless legs, and offering iron if ferritin is 75 or below or transferrin saturation is under 20%. It says these cut-offs come from expert consensus and have not been tested directly.
claims.qualifications: Label it as a 2025 US guideline. AASM reports ferritin in ng/mL; UK laboratories report micrograms per litre, which is numerically the same unit (1 ng/mL = 1 microgram/L). Test in the morning, off iron for 24 hours. Between 75 and 100, the guideline suggests intravenous iron only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Thresholds are consensus, 'not been empirically tested'. UK guidance was not opened (see C11-22-g).

numbers.meaning: ferritin at or below which oral or IV iron is suggested in adults with RLS (consensus)
transferrin saturation below which iron is suggested
ferritin range where only IV iron is suggested
avoid iron-containing supplements and foods before the morning blood test

claims.claim: Normal iron results do not rule out benefit from iron in restless legs: the iron thresholds differ from those used in the general population.
claims.supporting_passage: Discussion (page 148): "In the general population, iron administration is generally recommended for those with evidence of iron deficiency as determined by serum iron studies. In RLS, however, it is likely brain iron deficiency, particularly in specific brain regions, is involved in its pathophysiology. Therefore, there are patients with normal serum iron studies who benefit from iron administration, which is borne out by the clinical trials." Good Practice Statement: "These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population."
claims.location: Discussion, page 148 (Undermind read_pdfs); Abstract, Good Practice Statement
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: In restless legs, a ferritin that is normal by the usual standard can still be low enough for iron to help. The US guideline says some people with normal iron results benefit from iron, and it uses a higher cut-off (75) than for iron deficiency in general.
claims.qualifications: Do not state specific laboratory reference ranges (not sourced). The guideline's reasoning about brain iron is a proposed mechanism ('it is likely').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The cut-offs themselves are untested consensus.

numbers.meaning: ferritin cut-off (ng/mL, same as micrograms/L) in the AASM good practice statement

claims.claim: The first step in managing restless legs is addressing aggravating factors: alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic and antidopaminergic medicines, and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea.
claims.supporting_passage: "The first step in the management of RLS should be addressing exacerbating factors, such as alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic, antidopaminergic medications, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea." Future Directions (page 150): "RLS is often comorbid with mood, anxiety, and pain disorders, which present challenges to treatment because the most common treatments—serotonergic reuptake inhibitors—often worsen RLS."
claims.location: Abstract, Good Practice Statement 2; Future Directions, page 150
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: Before adding a medicine for restless legs, look for things that make it worse: alcohol, caffeine, sedating antihistamines, many antidepressants (serotonergic ones), medicines that block dopamine (such as some anti-sickness drugs and antipsychotics), and untreated sleep apnoea.
claims.qualifications: Good practice statement (expert consensus). Examples of drug classes in brackets are the post's plain-English glosses of the guideline's categories; keep them as examples, not a complete list.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: The AASM now recommends gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin (strong, moderate certainty) and suggests against the standard use of levodopa, pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine (conditional), mainly because of augmentation, a treatment-induced worsening of restless legs over months to years.
claims.supporting_passage: "2. In adults with RLS, the AASM recommends the use of gabapentin over no gabapentin (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 3. In adults with RLS, the AASM recommends the use of pregabalin over no pregabalin (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence)." "12. In adults with RLS, the AASM suggests against the standard use of pramipexole (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). Remarks: pramipexole may be used to treat RLS in patients who place a higher value on the reduction of restless legs symptoms with short-term use and a lower value on adverse effects with long-term use (particularly augmentation)." Introduction (page 139): "Augmentation clinically describes a gradual worsening of RLS symptom intensity and duration, which occurs over months to years of exposure to dopaminergic agents." "Augmentation manifests as 1 or more of the following: earlier symptom onset than prior to dopaminergic treatment (eg, from nighttime to daytime), reduced latency to symptom onset with sedentary activities, and/or extension to other areas of the body." Discussion (page 148): "Thus, in balancing the risks of augmentation against the clinical benefits of dopamine agonists or levodopa, this CPG suggests against their use as standard treatments in adults with RLS."
claims.location: Abstract, Recommendations 1 to 3 and 11 to 14 with remarks; Introduction page 139; Discussion page 148
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: The 2025 US guideline now puts gabapentin and pregabalin first among medicines, and advises against using pramipexole, ropinirole or rotigotine as standard treatment. The reason is augmentation: over months to years these drugs can make restless legs start earlier in the day, come on faster at rest and spread to other parts of the body.
claims.qualifications: The recommendations against dopamine agonists are conditional; the guideline allows them where short-term relief is valued over long-term risk. The guideline also strongly recommends IV ferric carboxymaltose when iron status is appropriate, and conditionally suggests opioids.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Dopamine agonists do work in the short term ('There is no argument that dopamine agonists have demonstrated short-term efficacy in clinical trials'). The guideline's text quotes US national data (2017 to 2018) that 60% of medication-treated people were still prescribed dopamine agonists; this figure was read only through Undermind and is US-specific.

claims.claim: Gabapentinoids cause somnolence and dizziness; in older people, the Beers Criteria advise dose reduction when creatinine clearance is below 60 mL/min, avoiding combination with opioids, and avoiding three or more CNS-active drugs (including gabapentinoids) because of falls and fracture risk; for people with a history of falls, antiepileptics are to be avoided except for seizures and mood disorders.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM (Recommendations 1 to 3): "Adverse effects included somnolence and dizziness." "Patients who are at a high risk of side effects with this class of medications may choose other treatment options." Discussion (page 148): "This class of medications can have adverse effects, including dizziness and somnolence, which may influence shared decision-making for prescribers and patients." Beers 2023 Table 6 (page 34): Gabapentin, CrCl <60, "CNS adverse effects", "Reduce dose", Moderate, Strong; Pregabalin, same. Table 5 (page 31): Opioids + Gabapentin, Pregabalin: "Increased risk of severe sedation-related adverse events, including respiratory depression and death." "Avoid; exceptions are when transitioning from opioid therapy to gabapentin or pregabalin, or when using gabapentinoids to reduce opioid dose, although caution should be used in all circumstances." Table 5: "Antiepileptics (including gabapentinoids)" ... "Any combination of ≥3 of these CNS-active drugs": "Increased risk of falls and of fracture"; "Avoid concurrent use of ≥3 CNS-active drugs". Table 3 (page 27), History of falls or fractures: Antiepileptics ... "May cause ataxia, impaired psychomotor function, syncope, or additional falls." Recommendation: "Avoid unless safer alternatives are not available. Antiepileptics: avoid except for seizures and mood disorders."
claims.location: AASM recommendation text pages 140 to 143 and Discussion page 148 (Undermind read_pdfs); Beers 2023 Tables 3, 5, 6, pages 27, 31, 34 (Undermind read_pdfs)
claims.pico_timeframe: AASM: adults with RLS, trials; Beers: adults 65 and over, US
claims.safe_wording: Gabapentin and pregabalin commonly cause sleepiness and dizziness. In older people, the Beers Criteria advise a lower dose when kidney function is reduced, avoiding them alongside opioids, and avoiding three or more drugs that act on the brain together because of falls and fractures. For someone who has already fallen, weigh this carefully before starting them.
claims.qualifications: The AASM guideline itself does not mention falls or older adults; the falls link comes from Beers. Beers Table 3 names 'Antiepileptics' (Table 5 states that antiepileptics include gabapentinoids); do not say Beers bans gabapentinoids for restless legs. Beers is a US list; 'avoid' is not an absolute contraindication.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Tension between AASM (gabapentinoids recommended) and Beers (antiepileptics to be avoided after falls except for seizures or mood disorders) should be stated as a trade-off, not resolved.

numbers.meaning: kidney function at which Beers advises reducing gabapentin and pregabalin dose
number of concurrent CNS-active drugs Beers advises avoiding

claims.claim: UK guidance (NICE CKS) may still list dopamine agonists and may differ from the US guideline.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary (pages not opened): "The NICE CKS guidance recommends gabapentinoids as first-line treatment, with a statement that due to the high incidence of augmentation and the risk of impulse control disorders, dopamine agonists should not be first-line treatment." "Iron replacement therapy is recommended if serum ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L".
claims.pico_timeframe: UK primary care guidance; date not established
claims.safe_wording: Do not describe UK guidance in the post. Label the source as a 2025 US guideline. If a UK comparison is wanted, it needs NICE CKS opened first.
claims.qualifications: search_extract only; the summary could not be tied to one official page with certainty. It suggests UK guidance has moved in the same direction, contrary to the judge's concern, but this is unverified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified.

claims.claim: Specialist guidance recommends that people with obstructive sleep apnoea who use CPAP continue using it during a hospital stay for surgery, before and after the operation, and that the hospital either has equipment available or the patient brings their own.
claims.supporting_passage: "Recommendation 3.1.4: Patients Should Continue to Wear Their PAP Device at Appropriate Times During Their Stay in the Hospital, Both Preoperatively and Postoperatively (Level of Evidence: Moderate. Grade of Recommendation: Strong for)" "We recommend the continued use of PAP therapy at previously prescribed settings during periods of sleep while hospitalized. Adjustments may need to be made to the settings to account for perioperative changes, such as facial swelling, upper airway edema, fluid shifts, pharmacotherapy, and respiratory function. It should be noted that PAP therapy is not an alternative to appropriate monitoring." "Recommendation 3.1.3: We Suggest That Facilities Should Consider Having PAP Equipment for Perioperative Use Available or Have the Patient Bring Their Own PAP Equipment to the Surgical Facility (Level of Evidence: Low. Grade of Recommendation: Strong for)" "Local institutional policies may determine how this matter is to be handled as logistical capabilities and expertise may vary."
claims.location: Section 3.1, Recommendations 3.1.3 (page 463) and 3.1.4 (page 464); Executive Summary page 467 (Undermind read_pdfs of published PDF)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with diagnosed OSA using PAP, having surgery; perioperative hospital stay; guideline 2016
claims.safe_wording: Anaesthesia and sleep specialists advise that people who use CPAP keep using it in hospital around an operation, before and after. Their guidance says hospitals should either have a machine available or ask patients to bring their own, so take yours, with the mask, tubing and power lead, and tell the staff.
claims.qualifications: The guidance is for surgical admissions (Society of Anesthesia and Sleep Medicine, 2016, North American-led, not UK). Extending the advice to unplanned medical admissions is a reasonable practical suggestion, not a guideline statement; word it as advice ('if you are admitted unexpectedly, ask someone to bring it in'). Local hospital policy decides how equipment is handled; settings may need adjusting after surgery.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. The ASA 2014 guideline could not be opened (no abstract, PDF unavailable).

claims.claim: Opioid painkillers and sedatives may increase the risk of breathing problems in people with obstructive sleep apnoea.
claims.supporting_passage: "2.2.1 Recommendation: Patients with OSA may be at increased risk for adverse respiratory events from the use of opioid medications." "Level of evidence: Low; Grade of recommendation: Weak". Executive Summary (page 980): "Given the respiratory depressant effects of opioids, patients with OSA may be at increased risk for respiratory complications from the use of these analgesic drugs." Rationale (page 974): "In a volunteer study, Bernards et al directly demonstrated that opioid administration during sleep increased the number of central apneas, leading to decreased saturation levels in patients with OSA versus those without OSA." "In summary, limited literature suggests that patients with OSA may be at increased risk for opioid-related respiratory adverse events. However, high-quality evidence to support and prove this notion is largely lacking". "2.6.1 Recommendation: Patients with OSA may be at increased risk for adverse respiratory events from intravenous benzodiazepine sedation. Intravenous benzodiazepine sedation should be used with caution." (Level of evidence: Moderate; Grade: Weak)
claims.location: Sections 2.2 (pages 973 to 974) and 2.6 (page 977); Executive Summary page 980 (Undermind read_pdfs of published PDF)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with OSA, perioperative opioids and IV benzodiazepine sedation; mostly observational evidence
claims.safe_wording: Strong painkillers such as morphine-type drugs, and some sedatives, may make breathing problems more likely in people with sleep apnoea. The evidence for this is limited, which is one more reason to keep using CPAP in hospital and to tell staff you have sleep apnoea.
claims.qualifications: Use 'may'; the guideline grades the opioid evidence as low and the recommendation as weak. Do not claim CPAP prevents opioid-related harm (not studied here; the 2016 guideline says 'PAP therapy is not an alternative to appropriate monitoring').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High-quality evidence is lacking, as the guideline says.

claims.claim: UK hospitals may need to safety-check a patient's own CPAP machine before it is used on the ward.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Phrase only as a question to ask: 'Ask whether the ward needs to check your machine before you use it.' Do not state that a check is required.
claims.qualifications: No UK hospital policy or guideline was opened. The SASM guideline says local institutional policies decide how equipment is handled.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable.

claims.claim: In a US screening of 492 nursing home residents, 339 had excessive daytime sleeping.
claims.supporting_passage: "Residents were screened for excessive daytime sleeping (asleep > or = 15% of daytime observations) and nighttime sleep disruption (asleep < 80% of nighttime hours, according to wrist actigraphy). Four hundred ninety-two residents were screened; 339 had excessive daytime sleeping. Of these, 133 had nighttime sleep disruption and consented to participate"
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of four Los Angeles nursing homes screened for a trial; published 2005
claims.safe_wording: In four US nursing homes, about 7 in 10 residents screened for a sleep study (339 of 492) were asleep in at least 15 in 100 daytime checks.
claims.qualifications: Screening sample for a trial in four Los Angeles homes, not a prevalence estimate for UK care homes. Define 'excessive daytime sleeping' as asleep in 15% or more of daytime observations.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Old (published 2005), US only.

numbers.meaning: residents screened who had excessive daytime sleeping (asleep in 15% or more of daytime observations); about 69 in 100
threshold of daytime observations asleep used to define excessive daytime sleeping

claims.claim: Night-time noise and light changes are associated with residents waking; in a US trial, noise peaks above 50 dB occurred in an average of 83 two-minute intervals a night before intervention, but reducing noise and light did not improve most sleep measures.
claims.supporting_passage: "The sleep of nursing home residents is fragmented by frequent awakening episodes associated, at least in part, with environmental variables, including noise and light changes." "Noise was reduced significantly, from an average of 83 intervals per night with peak noises recorded above 50 dBs to an average of 58 intervals per night in the group that received the initial intervention ... light changes were reduced from an average of four per night per resident to two per night (P < .001). Despite these significant changes in the environmental variables, there was a significant differential improvement in the intervention group on only two night sleep measures: awakening associated with a combination of noise plus light (P < .001) and awakening associated with light (P < .001)." "The significant reductions in noise and light events resulting from the intervention did not lead to significant improvements in the day sleep and most night sleep measures."
claims.pico_timeframe: 267 incontinent residents, eight US nursing homes / staff feedback on noise, noise abatement, individualised night incontinence care, 7pm to 6am / delayed-intervention controls / actigraphy awakenings, noise and light monitors; published 1999
claims.safe_wording: In US nursing homes, residents' night-time waking was linked with noise and changes in light. Cutting noise and light reduced the waking linked to light, but on its own did not improve most measures of sleep.
claims.qualifications: The opening statement is the paper's background; the measured finding is fewer awakenings associated with light and with noise plus light. Old US data; do not claim that quieter nights alone improve sleep.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors suggest noise may not have been reduced enough; a correlation between noise change and sleep change was r = -0.29.

numbers.meaning: average two-minute intervals per night with noise peaks above 50 dB, before and during intervention (intervention group)
average light changes per night per resident, before and during intervention

claims.claim: Routine night-time continence checks can wake residents; tailoring the check schedule to each resident's skin risk, and giving care when residents are found awake, reduced care-related awakenings without harming skin. Wet episodes themselves rarely woke residents.
claims.supporting_passage: Schnelle 1998: "A previous study of incontinent NH residents demonstrated that noise from the staff and other residents and light and noise from staff-initiated incontinence care routines were associated with waking episodes." "Subjects were assigned to a 2- or 4-hour incontinence care schedule based on each resident's risk of skin problems using objective data of spontaneous body movements at night and skin health during baseline, and the research staff provided incontinence care if residents were found awake." "Awakenings due to light and sound associated with incontinence care were significantly reduced during the intervention phases (p < .001), and there were no adverse changes in skin health or on most risk factors associated with skin (e.g., exposure to moisture, body turns)." Ouslander 1998: "Recordings covered 403 nights, during which 1715 awakenings from 10 consecutive minutes of sleep were detected as were 1168 incontinent episodes. Only 4% of the awakenings were associated with an incontinence episode". Ostaszkiewicz 2015: "Most residents were checked overnight. This practice was underpinned by staffs' concern that residents were intractably incontinent and at risk of pressure injuries. ... Decisions were also influenced by beliefs about limited staff-to-resident ratios." "Night-time continence care should be audited to ensure decisions are based on residents' preferences, skin health, sleep/wake status, ability to move in bed, and the frequency, severity and type of residents' actual incontinence."
claims.pico_timeframe: US nursing home residents with incontinence (1998 trial and case series); two Australian facilities (2015 qualitative)
claims.safe_wording: In US nursing home studies, being wet rarely woke residents: about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings were linked to a wet episode. The light and noise of routine night-time continence checks were linked with waking. Setting each person's checks by their own skin risk, and giving care when they were already awake, cut care-related waking with no harm to skin.
claims.qualifications: Small, old US studies with care given by research staff; the tailored schedule was 2- or 4-hourly by skin risk, not 'no checks'. Night checks can be needed for skin and safety; frame questions as asking how checks are planned for each person, not implying checks are wrong. Do not quote the Australian 'commonly disrupts sleep' sentence as a finding (background).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Ouslander 1998 authors caution about the technology used to detect sleep and wetness.

numbers.meaning: individualised check intervals assigned by skin risk (Schnelle 1998)
share of 1715 awakenings over 403 nights associated with an incontinence episode (Ouslander 1998)

claims.claim: In UK care homes, staff settle residents into dark, quiet bedrooms and describe insufficient night staffing as a barrier to good night care.
claims.supporting_passage: Webster 2022: "In the evening, staff settled residents into dark, quiet, comfortable bedrooms often after a snack. When residents woke at night, they gave them caffeinated tea or food, considered possible pain and discomfort, and reassured residents they were safe. ... Staff found minimising daytime napping difficult, described insufficient staffing at night to attend to reorient and guide awake residents and said residents frequently did not know it was night-time." "Some common techniques, such as caffeinated drinks, may be counterproductive." Nunez 2017: "Thematic analysis revealed eight key themes in the management of sleep disturbance in people with dementia living in care homes: current night-time care practices, dissonance in perceived causes of sleep disturbances, inconsistencies in treatment options, insufficient staffing levels, working relationships between shifts, nurse burden and responsibility, communication as a critical challenge, connecting with residents and one overarching theme of balance."
claims.pico_timeframe: 18 staff in four UK care homes (2022); staff and family carers in five South London care homes (2017); residents with dementia
claims.safe_wording: UK care home staff interviewed about nights describe settling residents into dark, quiet rooms, and say there are too few night staff to help residents who wake.
claims.qualifications: Small qualitative studies about residents with dementia; they describe practice and constraints, not measured effects on sleep. Use to frame questions respectfully (the questions are about the home's plan and staffing, not blame on night staff).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: nurses and care assistants interviewed in four UK care homes (Webster 2022)

claims.claim: UK care standards (CQC Regulation 9 in England; Health and Social Care Standards in Scotland) require care that reflects residents' preferences, including daily routines such as bedtimes.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite regulations or standards. The point that residents and families may ask about bedtimes and who decides them can stand as a values statement ('You can ask...'), not as a legal requirement.
claims.qualifications: Official pages could not be opened. A copy of the Scottish Health and Social Care Standards exists in Drive only as a production in a legal case bundle (file titled HS25000051-Pro 191); it was not opened, in line with the rule on confidential case files. CQC Regulation 9 applies to England only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable.

claims.claim: A randomised trial in four Los Angeles nursing homes gave 118 residents (mean age 86.9) with excessive daytime sleeping and disrupted night sleep five days and nights of less daytime time in bed, at least 30 minutes of daily sunlight, more physical activity, a structured bedtime routine and less night-time noise and light, compared with usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: "Randomized, controlled trial. Four nursing homes in the Los Angeles area." "120 completed baseline assessments, and 118 (77% female, mean age 86.9, 90% non-Hispanic white) were randomized to intervention versus usual care." "Five consecutive days and nights of efforts to decrease daytime in-bed time, 30 minutes or more of daily sunlight exposure, increased physical activity, structured bedtime routine, and efforts to decrease nighttime noise and light." "Seventy-two consecutive hours of wrist actigraphy (nighttime sleep) and structured behavioral observations (daytime sleep and participation in social and physical activities and social conversation) at baseline and repeated at follow-up while the intervention or usual care condition was in place."
claims.pico_timeframe: 118 US nursing home residents / five-day multicomponent programme / usual care / actigraphic night sleep and observed daytime sleep and activity / measured during the intervention period; published 2005
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in four nursing homes, 118 residents (average age 87) who slept a lot by day and poorly at night had five days of: less time in bed during the day, at least 30 minutes of daylight, more activity, a regular bedtime routine and quieter, darker nights.
claims.qualifications: State the five-day duration and that outcomes were measured while the programme was running; no data on lasting effect. 90% non-Hispanic white, US, 2005.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C11-07-d.

numbers.meaning: residents randomised
mean age in years
consecutive days and nights of intervention
minimum daily sunlight exposure
measurement period at baseline and follow-up

claims.claim: Night-time sleep changed little: the only effect was a modest difference in the length of night-time awakenings (10.6 to 9.8 minutes with the programme versus 9.8 to 13.8 minutes with usual care); no significant effect on percentage of the night asleep or number of awakenings.
claims.supporting_passage: "The only effect on nighttime sleep was a modest decrease in mean duration of nighttime awakenings in intervention participants (10.6 minutes at baseline, 9.8 minutes at follow-up) versus an increase in controls (9.8 minutes at baseline, 13.8 minutes at follow-up) (F=4.27, P=.04). There were no significant effects on percentage of nighttime sleep or number of nighttime awakenings."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-07-a; wrist actigraphy
claims.safe_wording: Night sleep barely changed. The trial found no clear difference in how much of the night residents slept or how often they woke; each spell awake at night was slightly shorter with the programme (about 10 minutes, against about 14 minutes with usual care).
claims.qualifications: Describe the small awakening-length difference; do not call the night-time result a failure or 'no effect'. Non-significant results mean no clear difference, not proof of none.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with Ouslander 2006 (C11-07-d).

numbers.meaning: mean length of night-time awakenings, intervention, baseline to follow-up
mean length of night-time awakenings, usual care, baseline to follow-up

claims.claim: Daytime sleeping fell from 32% to 21% of daytime observations with the programme versus 32% to 30% with usual care; participation in social and physical activities and social conversation increased.
claims.supporting_passage: "There was a significant decrease in daytime sleeping in intervention participants (32% of daytime observations asleep at baseline, 21% at follow-up), with no change in controls (32% at baseline, 30% at follow-up; F=20.68, P<.001). Intervention participants had increased participation in social (F=22.42, P<.001) and physical (F=12.65, P=.001) activities and social conversation (F=5.04, P=.03)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-07-a; structured daytime behavioural observations
claims.safe_wording: By day the picture changed. With the programme, residents were asleep in 21 of every 100 daytime checks, down from 32. With usual care it went from 32 to 30. Residents in the programme also took part in more social and physical activities and more conversation.
claims.qualifications: Percentages are of structured daytime observations, not of people. Activity results reported as statistical tests only (no percentages in the abstract), so do not invent figures for them. Measured during the five-day programme.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No longer-term follow-up.

numbers.meaning: daytime observations asleep, intervention, baseline to follow-up
daytime observations asleep, usual care, baseline to follow-up

claims.claim: Other evidence: a similar multicomponent programme in eight US nursing homes had no effect on night sleep, and a Cochrane review found only low-certainty evidence for non-drug sleep interventions in people with dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: Ouslander 2006: "There were no significant differences in any of the primary actigraphic sleep outcome measures between the intervention and control group after the immediate-intervention phase of the trial." "This multicomponent, nonpharmacological intervention conducted by trained research staff had no effect on nighttime sleep in this sample of nursing home patients." Wilfling 2023: "We included 19 randomised controlled trials with 1335 participants ... Fourteen studies were conducted in nursing homes ... Fourteen studies were conducted in the US." "Multimodal interventions may modestly increase total nocturnal sleep time and may modestly reduce the total wake time at night, but may result in little to no difference in number of awakenings (low-certainty evidence)." "At present, no single or multimodal intervention can be clearly identified as suitable for widespread implementation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Ouslander: eight US nursing homes, controlled trial, 2006; Wilfling: 19 RCTs, people with dementia and sleep problems, search to January 2022
claims.safe_wording: A similar programme in eight other US nursing homes also did not change night sleep, and a 2023 Cochrane review rated the evidence for non-drug sleep programmes in dementia as low certainty.
claims.qualifications: Ouslander 2006 did not report daytime sleeping as a primary outcome in the abstract, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the daytime result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Supports the 'nights change little' reading; the daytime benefit rests on one small, short trial.

numbers.meaning: residents who completed the intervention in Ouslander 2006
Cochrane review size (14 in nursing homes, 14 in the US)

candidates.reason: Bruck 2009 abstract gives all the figures (n = 38, aged 18 to 80, deep sleep, laboratory; standard 3100 Hz alarm 56%, 520 Hz 92% at 75 dBA; shakers 80 to 84% as purchased; strobe 27%). The UK route is supported by 2025 papers: all English fire and rescue services offer Home Fire Safety Visits (James and Clark) and UK services routinely deliver them (Hampton). Required wording: say who was studied (all adult ages, not an older-adult sample); frame hearing aids conditionally (abstract does not say whether aids were worn); do not recommend buying a 520 Hz alarm (UK availability not checked); state specialist alarm provision only as a question to ask (search_extract only); advise checking that any kit includes a vibrating pad, since the strobe alone woke 27 in 100. Judge suggested this may fit C14 (hearing) better; editor's call.

All claims verified in the AASM 2025 guideline (abstract, recommendation remarks, Introduction and Discussion via PDF) and Beers 2023 tables. The sharpen angle is directly supported: 'there are patients with normal serum iron studies who benefit from iron administration' and the thresholds are 'different than for the general population'. Must label as a 2025 US guideline, say the iron cut-offs are untested consensus, note the recommendations against dopamine agonists are conditional, and present gabapentinoid harms in older people (sleepiness, dizziness; Beers: reduce dose if CrCl below 60, avoid with opioids, avoid 3 or more CNS-active drugs; antiepileptics to be avoided after falls except for seizures or mood disorders) as a trade-off. Do not describe UK (NICE CKS) guidance: only a search extract, which suggests it has moved the same way.

SASM 2016 (opened in full) recommends continued PAP use during the hospital stay before and after surgery (moderate evidence, strong) and that facilities have equipment or patients bring their own (low evidence, strong). SASM 2018 says people with OSA may be at increased risk of breathing problems from opioids (low evidence, weak) and from IV benzodiazepine sedation. Wording must use 'may' for the drug risk, attribute the CPAP advice to surgical guidance, and give the emergency-admission and safety-check points as practical suggestions or questions, not facts (no UK hospital policy found). The CPAP-nocturia optional claim was not checked and should be left out. ASA 2014 could not be opened and is not needed.

The evidence supports the questions but not the stronger framing. Supported: many US nursing home residents sleep a lot by day (339 of 492 screened); night noise and light are linked with waking; routine continence checks wake residents more than wetness does, and a tailored 2- or 4-hourly schedule cut care-related waking without skin harm (small, old US studies with research staff); UK staff describe dark, quiet rooms and too few night staff. Not supported: that homes which individualise bedtimes protect sleep (no evidence found), that quieter nights alone improve sleep (Schnelle 1999 found most sleep measures unchanged), and the UK care standards (not opened; Drive copy is a legal case production and was not opened).
candidates.revised_angle: Ask this: four questions for a care home visit or review about nights, framed to invite the home to explain its plan rather than to accuse night staff. 1) How are night checks planned for each person, and can they be changed? (US studies: checks timed by each person's skin risk cut waking without harming skin.) 2) How is continence care done at night if someone is asleep? 3) How are noise and lights kept down, and what happens if someone is awake at 3am? 4) What time do residents go to bed, and who decides? (a values question about choice; no sleep evidence claimed). Make clear that some checks are needed for skin and safety, that the evidence is small and mostly old and American, and that UK staff report too few night staff. Do not cite regulations.

candidates.reason: Reserve. All figures verified in the Alessi 2005 abstract: 118 residents, mean age 86.9, four Los Angeles homes, five days; night sleep changed little (awakening length 10.6 to 9.8 minutes versus 9.8 to 13.8; no significant effect on percentage asleep or number of awakenings); daytime sleeping 32% to 21% of observations versus 32% to 30%; more social and physical activity and conversation. Ouslander 2006 (no effect on night sleep with a similar programme) and Cochrane 2023 (low certainty) are consistent with the 'nights change little' reading. Must state five-day duration, measurement during the programme, US 2005 population (90% non-Hispanic white), and describe the small night-time difference rather than calling it a failure. Shares its source with C11-27 (claim C11-27-a); if both are used, avoid repeating the 339 of 492 figure.
